name: Dark Delft Blue
lede: Dark Delft Blue is a dark, greyed blue-green carried in our library by three independent systems at once: Ridgway's 1912 naturalist chart, the 1955 ISCC-NBS standard, and a Japanese traditional name, Noshimehana-iro.

sections.title: Three systems, one block of color
sections.body:
Robert Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature*, a chart built for naturalists describing specimens, plots a swatch in this neighborhood on plate XLII, hue 45, tone m, and again on plate XLVIII at a slightly different hue and tone; both plates in our scanned copy have aged, so the readings are approximate [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS system separately classes the same block of color, under its block 183, as a dark blue [2].

Our library also carries the Japanese name Noshimehana-iro for a very close color, written 熨斗目花色; the kanji combine a term for a striped kimono weave (*noshime*) with "flower color," and the library glosses the whole, a little literally, as "iron head flower color" [3]. No book consulted here independently confirms when that Japanese name entered use, so its date is undocumented [3]. The nearest named colors on file are [[dark-teal-grey]], [[saccardo-s-slate]] and [[dusky-orient-blue]], at 3, 3 and 3.7 ΔE [1][2][3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A color within range of this swatch appears in 310 of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, about 1.3 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 134 [4]. That makes it more common than 63 percent of the named colors we track [4].

It peaks in the 1400s, present in 14 of 945 paintings from that century, 2.2 times the expected rate [4]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in nearly half the paintings that carry it, the kind of tone lightness ranking alone would not flag [4]. The earliest dated appearance we have is 1260, 652 years before Ridgway's 1912 chart, which is a reminder that a color match in an old, varnished photograph is a look-alike hue, not proof that anyone at the time used this name or dye, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [4].
